Main.sentence: Trickle-down economics , also known as the horse-and-sparrow theory ,  describes government economic policies that disproportionately favor the upper tier of the economic spectrum (wealthy individuals and large corporations).

The term has been used broadly by critics of ___E:supply-side economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply-side_economics)___ to refer to ___E:taxing and spending policies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_policy)___ by governments that, intentionally or not, result in widening ___E:income inequality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_inequality)___ ; it has also been used in critical references to ___E:neoliberalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoliberalism)___ .
These critics reject the notion that spending by this elite group would "trickle down" to those who are less fortunate and lead to economic growth that will eventually benefit the economy as a whole.

While criticisms have existed since at least the 19th century, the term "trickle-down economics" was popularized by ___E:Democrats in the US U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ to derogate ___E:Reaganomics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaganomics)___ and its reduction in the top marginal tax rates.

Major examples of what critics have called "trickle-down economics" in the US include the ___E:Reagan tax cuts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagan_tax_cuts)___ ,  the ___E:Bush tax cuts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_tax_cuts)___ , and in UK include ___E:Margaret Thatcher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher)___ 's economic policies in the 1980s and ___E:Liz Truss U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Truss)___ 's ___E:mini-budget tax cuts of 2022 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_2022_United_Kingdom_mini-budget)___ .

In 1896, United States ___E:Democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ presidential candidate ___E:William Jennings Bryan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan)___ claimed in his ___E:Cross of Gold speech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Gold_speech)___ that his opposition based their policies on the idea that the success of the rich would "leak through" to the lower classes, stating: "There are those who believe that, if you will only legislate to make the well-to-do prosperous, their prosperity will leak through on those below."

Author and political commentator ___E:William Safire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Safire)___ , in his political dictionary, defined "trickle-down theory" as "The idea that aid to corporations will seep through to employees and irrigate the economy."

___E:William J. Bennett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Bennett)___ credits humorist and social commentator ___E:Will Rogers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Rogers)___ for coining the term and observed in 2007 its persistent use throughout the decades since.

In a 1932 column criticizing ___E:Herbert Hoover's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover)___ policies and approach to ___E:The Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Depression)___ , Rogers wrote: "The money was all appropriated for the top in the hopes that it would trickle down to the needy.
Mr. Hoover was an engineer.
He knew that water trickles down. Put it uphill and let it go and it will reach the driest little spot."

In 1983, ___E:H. W. Arndt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._W._Arndt)___ wrote that Indian nationalist and statesman ___E:Jawaharlal Nehru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru)___ may have been the first to use the term in an economic (rather than political context) when he stated in 1933 "the exploitation of India and other countries brought so much wealth to England that some of it trickled down to the working class and their standard of living rose."

After leaving the ___E:presidency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States)___ , Democrat ___E:Lyndon B. Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson)___ alleged " ___E:Republicans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ ... simply don't know how to manage the economy.

They're so busy operating the trickle-down theory, giving the richest corporations the biggest break, that the whole thing goes ___E:to hell in a handbasket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_hell_in_a_handbasket)___ ."  ___E:Samuel Rosenman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Rosenman)___ , a Democratic presidential speechwriter under ___E:Franklin D. Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt)___ and ___E:Harry Truman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Truman)___ , and coiner of the term " ___E:New Deal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal)___ ", wrote that "trickle down policies" had been prevalent in American government since 1921.
Ronald Reagan launched his 1980 campaign for the presidency on a platform advocating for ___E:supply-side economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply-side_economics)___ .

During the ___E:1980 Republican Party presidential primaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries)___ , ___E:George H. W. Bush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush)___ had derided Reagan's economic approach as "voodoo economics".

Following Reagan's election, the "trickle-down" reached wide circulation with the publication of "The Education of David Stockman", a December 1981 interview of Reagan's incoming ___E:Office of Management and Budget U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Management_and_Budget)___ director ___E:David Stockman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Stockman)___ , in the magazine ___E:Atlantic Monthly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic)___ .

In the interview, Stockman expressed doubts about ___E:supply side economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply_side_economics)___ , telling journalist ___E:William Greider U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Greider)___ that the ___E:Kemp–Roth Tax Cut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Recovery_Tax_Act_of_1981)___ was a way to rebrand a tax cut for the top income bracket to make it easier to pass into law.  Stockman said that "It's kind of hard to sell 'trickle down,' so the supply-side formula was the only way to get a tax policy that was really 'trickle down.' Supply-side is 'trickle-down' theory."    Reagan administration officials including ___E:Michael Deaver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Deaver)___ wanted Stockman to be fired in response to his comments, but he was ultimately kept on in exchange for a private apology.

Political opponents of the ___E:Reagan administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagan_administration)___ soon seized on this language in an effort to brand the administration as caring only about the wealthy.

In 1982, ___E:John Kenneth Galbraith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kenneth_Galbraith)___ wrote the "trickle-down economics" that Stockman was referring to was previously known under the name "horse-and-sparrow theory", the idea that feeding a horse a huge amount of oats results in some of the feed passing through for lucky sparrows to eat.

While the term "trickle-down" is commonly used to refer to income benefits, it is sometimes used to refer to the idea of ___E:positive externalities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality)___ arising from technological innovation or increased trade. ___E:Arthur Okun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Melvin_Okun)___ ,  and separately ___E:William Baumol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Baumol)___ ,  for example, have used the term to refer to the flow of the benefits of innovation, which do not accrue entirely to the "great entrepreneurs and inventors", but trickle down to the masses.
And Nobel laureate economist ___E:Paul Romer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Romer)___ used the term in reference to the impact on wealth from tariff changes.
The ___E:Laffer curve U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laffer_curve)___ is often cited by proponents of trickle-down policy.

In the US, ___E:Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ tax plans and policies have been labeled "trickle-down economics", including the ___E:Reagan tax cuts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagan_tax_cuts)___ and the ___E:Bush tax cuts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_tax_cuts)___ .  [citation needed] In each of the aforementioned tax reforms, taxes were cut across all income brackets, but the biggest reductions were given to the highest income earners,  although the ___E:Reagan Era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagan_Era)___ tax reforms also introduced the ___E:earned income tax credit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earned_income_tax_credit)___ which has received bipartisan praise for poverty reduction and is largely why the bottom half of workers pay no federal income tax.

In the ___E:1992 presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election)___ , ___E:independent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politician)___ candidate ___E:Ross Perot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Perot)___ also referred to trickle-down economics as "political voodoo".

In the same election, during a presidential town hall debate, ___E:Bill Clinton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton)___ blamed trickle-down economics for the declining economic conditions in America, saying that "...we've had 12 years of trickle-down economics.
We've gone from first to twelfth in the world in wages.
We've had four years where we’ve produced no private-sector jobs. Most people are working harder for less money than they were making 10 years ago.".

The political campaign group, ___E:Tax Justice Network U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Justice_Network)___ has used the term referring broadly to wealth inequality in its criticisms of ___E:tax havens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_havens)___ .

In 2013, ___E:Pope Francis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis)___ condemned "trickle-down theories" in his ___E:apostolic exhortation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_exhortation)___ Evangelii gaudium , saying that "Some people continue to defend trickle-down theories which assume that economic growth, encouraged by a free market, will inevitably succeed in bringing about greater justice and inclusiveness in the world.

This opinion, which has never been confirmed by the facts, expresses a crude and naïve trust in the goodness of those wielding ___E:economic power U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_power)___ and in the sacralized workings of the prevailing economic system."

In New Zealand, ___E:Damien O'Connor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damien_O%27Connor)___ , an ___E:MP U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(New_Zealand))___ from the ___E:Labour Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)___ , called trickle-down economics "the rich pissing on the poor" in the Labour Party campaign launch video for the ___E:2011 general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_New_Zealand_general_election)___ .

In a ___E:2016 US presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_US_presidential_election)___ candidates debate, ___E:Hillary Clinton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton)___ accused ___E:Donald Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)___ of supporting the "most extreme" version of trickle-down economics with his tax plan, calling it "trumped-up trickle-down" as a pun on his name.  In his ___E:speech to a joint session of Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Joe_Biden_speech_to_a_joint_session_of_Congress)___ on April 28, 2021, US President ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ stated that "trickle-down economics has never worked".
Biden has continued to be critical of trickle-down.

A Columbia journal article comparing a failed UK ___E:Enterprise Zone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enterprise_Zone)___ proposal to later US proposals references them as a form of trickle-down policy where lower regulatory and tax burdens were aimed at wealthier developers with the hope they would benefit residents.

Nobel laureate ___E:Paul Krugman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman)___ states that despite the narrative of trickle-down style tax cuts, the effective tax rate of the top 1% of earners has failed to change very much.  Political commentator ___E:Robert Reich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Reich)___ has implicated institutions such as ___E:The Heritage Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Heritage_Foundation)___ , ___E:Cato Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cato_Institute)___ , and ___E:Club for Growth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_for_Growth)___ for promoting what he considers to be a discredited idea.  Kansas governor and politician ___E:Sam Brownback U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Brownback)___ 's 2018 tax cut package was widely labelled as an attempt at trickle-down economics.  ___E:Friedrich Hayek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Hayek)___ 's economic theories have also been described as trickle-down.

In 1983, ___E:H. W. Arndt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._W._Arndt)___ described the term as a myth, saying that no major economists of the 1950s assumed that wealth would accumulate among the rich and then spread to the poor.

Speaking on the ___E:US Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senate)___ floor in 1992, ___E:Hank Brown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Brown)___ (Republican senator for Colorado) objected to the use of the term for the policies of Ronald Reagan and ___E:George H. W. Bush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush)___ , saying that they have never advocated for it.  [non-primary source needed]

___E:Thomas Sowell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sowell)___ , a proponent of ___E:supply-side economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply-side_economics)___ , says that trickle-down economics have never been advocated by any economist, writing in his 2012 essay "Trickle Down" Theory and "Tax Cuts for the Rich" that "[t]he 'trickle-down' theory cannot be found in even the most voluminous scholarly studies of economic theories."  Sowell disagrees with the characterization of supply-side economics as trickle-down, saying that the economic theory of reducing marginal tax rates works in precisely the opposite direction: "Workers are always paid first and then profits flow upward later – if at all."   [better source needed]

Benjamin Lockwood, professor of business economics and public policy at ___E:Wharton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wharton_School)___ , said "The term ‘trickle-down economics’ doesn’t really represent a cohesive economic theory,” “It’s a term used, often negatively, to characterize the view that reducing taxes on the rich will benefit the non-rich.”
In 2022, the ___E:Liz Truss U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Truss)___ administration objected to characterizing its policies as "trickle-down economics".

Nobel laureate ___E:Joseph Stiglitz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stiglitz)___ wrote in 2015 that the post–World War II evidence does not support trickle-down economics, but rather " ___E:trickle-up economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trickle-up_economics)___ " whereby more money in the pockets of the poor or the middle benefits everyone.

In a 2020 research paper, economists David Hope and Julian Limberg analyzed data spanning 50 years from 18 countries, and found that tax cuts for the rich increased inequality in the short and medium term, and had no significant effect on real GDP per capita or employment in the short and medium term. According to the study, this shows that the tax cuts for the upper class did not trickle down to the broader economy.

From 1980 to 2016, a ___E:divergence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Divergence_(inequality))___ in the distribution of wealth was noted, with the top .01% of earners seeing a 600% change in real income, vs a 0% change in the bottom 99%, leading to the top 1% accruing 15% more of the total wealth pool, from a share of 15 to 30%.

A 2015 IMF staff discussion note by Era Dabla-Norris, Kalpana Kochhar, Nujin Suphaphiphat, Frantisek Ricka and Evridiki Tsounta suggests that lowering taxes on the top 20% could actually reduce growth.

Political scientists Brainard Guy Peters and Maximilian Lennart Nagel in 2020 described the 'trickle down' description of tax cuts for the wealthy and corporations stimulating economic growth that helps the less affluent as a "zombie idea", and stated that it has been the most enduring failed policy idea in American politics.

Some studies suggest a link between trickle-down economics and reduced growth, and some newspapers concluded that trickle-down economics does not promote jobs or growth, and that "policy makers shouldn't worry that raising taxes on the rich ... will harm their economies".
